name: Grace Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for making the time, Grace. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or parties, and everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a fuel tanker for a rural fuel distributor, mostly heating oil to farms and houses out in the villages, plus red diesel for tractors. I'm at the depot by six, load up, and do eight or nine drops, dragging the hose up driveways and finding tanks hidden behind hedges. I like the people, the old farmers who want a chat and a cup of tea. What wears me out is winter, when everyone runs dry in the same cold week.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Daniel, who works on his family's dairy farm, and the wedding is next August at our chapel. We've got a good amount saved, well over six months, because we've both been careful since school. I use a chatbot sometimes, mainly to sort the wedding seating plan, but I wouldn't trust it with anything that matters until I've seen it work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with things. People should stop worrying about computers and worry about whether the roads get gritted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thing on my mind isn't AI, it's heat pumps. More houses on my round are switching every year. The boss has started talking about running one tanker fewer. My job's safe for now and there's other tanker work about, but the heating oil side is slowly shrinking under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep my hazardous goods licence current, because that's what makes tanker drivers worth hiring. I'd ask about moving onto the farm diesel and forecourt deliveries, which are steadier than house heating oil. And we'd get married as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. Not about robots, about the oil round getting smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many customers on your round have switched?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one in ten in the last two years. Mrs Pryce at the end of the valley switched last spring and still rings me in November out of habit. It's quiet, but you notice it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that change your wedding or family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We'd still marry in August and live in the cottage on Daniel's farm. Kids in a couple of years, God willing. The oil round doesn't decide that.

say: I'd tell people to stop worrying about computers and **get on with things**.
I'd say **gritted roads** matter more than AI to people on my round.
think: My real worry is **heat pumps** shrinking the heating oil round.
The boss has talked about **one tanker fewer**, though my job is safe for now.
do: Keep my **hazardous goods licence** current to stay hireable.
Ask to move onto **farm diesel** and forecourt deliveries.
Go ahead with the **August wedding** as planned.
feel: She feels **a little uneasy** about the shrinking oil round, not about AI.
S0.quote: The thing on my mind isn't AI, it's heat pumps. More houses on my round are switching every year.
fieldNote: Her existing pressure is **energy change**, not automation.
She notices decline through **specific customers**, like a woman who still rings in winter.
Family plans, including **marriage and children**, are fixed and faith-framed.

steps.text: Renew the hazardous goods licence before it lapses
Ask the depot to move her onto farm diesel and forecourt runs
Marry Daniel next August and move into the farm cottage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office will change more than the tanker. Orders will come in through an app instead of the phone, and that'll be that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd bother me a bit. Half my round is old people who ring the office because they don't trust websites. Bev's the one who answers. If a computer takes the orders, those people get left out. My own job is mostly the hose and the driving, so I don't think it shrinks quickly, but I'd notice everything getting more rushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever the depot brought in, once a few of the others had tried it. I'd keep doing my round and the extra farm diesel work. If the ordering app made mistakes, I'd write them down and take them to the boss, because I'm the one who knocks on the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's fine, but the way we look after people would change, and not for the better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev in the office, and Mrs Pryce types who can't use an app. Bev's been there twenty-five years. I'd be sad to see her go, and the customers would be lost without her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to try the tools first. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen new kit fail. We had a new tank-gauge system two years ago that sent me to full tanks for a month. I'll use it when it's proved itself, not before.

think: I worry **older customers** who ring the office would be left out.

do: Learn the depot's **new systems** once others have tried them.
Keep doing my round plus the **farm diesel** runs.
Write down **app mistakes** and take them to the boss.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about how customers would be treated.
S1.quote: Half my round is old people who ring the office because they don't trust websites.
fieldNote: Her concern is **care for customers**, especially older rural people.
She's a **careful adopter**, burned by a faulty tank-gauge system before.
She'd act as an informal **quality check** on the new ordering app.

steps.text: Learn the depot's ordering app after colleagues have tested it
Keep driving the heating oil round and farm diesel runs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not right to turn people's lives upside down this fast, and I'd say families and churches will have to carry each other. I wouldn't be shy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think tanker driving is over for me by about 2031. A robot that can drive and handle the hose as well as me is the end of it. I'd be thirty-two, married, maybe with a baby, so that's a hard time to lose a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Daniel and his parents and talk about me joining the farm properly, maybe taking on the milk recording and the calves. We'd still marry in August, but we'd save harder and might wait a year longer for children. I'd keep driving every shift until the robots actually arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, with the farm and the savings, but it'd still feel like the ground going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't the farm be hit by robots too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, in the end. But a family farm is slower to change and it's ours, so we decide. I'd rather be working on something the family owns than for a company that'd swap me for a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at chapel about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been through hard times before and we've looked after each other. The minister would probably pray for the drivers. I'd ask people to share work where they can, not just pray.

I'd say **families and churches** will have to carry each other.
think: I think **tanker driving** ends for me by about 2031.
At thirty-two, married and maybe **with a baby**, losing a wage would hurt.
do: Talk with Daniel's parents about **joining the farm** properly.
**Save harder** and possibly wait a year longer for children.
Keep driving **every shift** until robots actually arrive.
feel: She feels **anxious**, with a plan but the ground shifting beneath her.
S2.quote: I'd rather be working on something the family owns than for a company that'd swap me for a machine.
fieldNote: Her safety net is **the family farm**, chosen for ownership and control.
She **delays children** rather than the wedding, keeping faith commitments.

steps.text: Ask Daniel's parents about taking on the calves and milk recording
Save harder and wait a year longer before having children
Drive every tanker shift offered until robots arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan this properly, and families should use it. I'd tell the younger drivers at the depot to think about what they'll do at thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I drive until about 2034. That's seven or eight good years. We'd be married, the kids would be little, and I'd have time to move onto the farm gradually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the tanker job and keep saving. I'd start helping on the farm at weekends, learning the dairy side properly. We'd put some savings into the new calf shed Daniel's dad wants to build, because that's our future too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more settled than the fast one. There's room to do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave the tanker job earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the depot started trialling robot tankers on our round. Until then, the wage is good and the farm can wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is putting your savings into the calf shed a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, yes. But I'd rather put money into cows I can see than into shares I don't understand. Daniel's dad has run that farm for forty years.

I'd tell **younger drivers** to think about their plans at thirty-five.
think: I think I drive until about **2034**.
Seven or eight years lets me **move onto the farm** gradually.

Put savings into the **new calf shed** on Daniel's family farm.

S3.quote: I'd rather put money into cows I can see than into shares I don't understand.
fieldNote: She trusts **tangible assets** like a calf shed over financial markets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a long time and nobody should panic. Plan, pray and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2039 I'd likely be on the farm anyway, with kids at school. This picture fits the life I already want. The driving would end around the time I'd want to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on driving, marry Daniel, and have children when we're ready. I'd move onto the farm part-time once the first baby comes. We'd invest in the farm over the years, maybe a milking robot when they're proven, which is funny when you think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a life I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a milking robot would be funny. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the robots would take my driving job and then I'd go and buy one for the cows. But that's how it is. If a machine helps the family farm, I'm for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The heating oil round is still shrinking. The depot might cut tankers before the robots even come. But with the farm and our savings, I'd manage.

I'd tell people to **plan and pray** and get on with it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. We'd have just married, maybe a baby on the way, and I'd be watching my wage disappear. What would help is the farm being able to take me on, and fair support for family businesses so they can afford to. Not money for nothing, but help for families to keep each other in work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old people. For some of the old people on my round, the oil delivery is the only visit they get all week. If a robot tanker fills their tank and drives off, who checks they're all right? That worries me more than my own job.

headlineQuote: For some of the old people on my round, the oil delivery is the only visit they get all week.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old fuel tanker driver** delivering heating oil to farms and villages.
She's **engaged to Daniel**, from a dairy farming family, and has strong savings.
Even in AI Plateau she's **uneasy** because heat pumps are shrinking her oil round.
In AGI by 2028 she plans to **join the family farm** and delay children.
With more warning, the farm becomes a **gradual move** that fits her family life.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, losing her wage just after marrying.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **support for family businesses** so they can keep relatives in work.
She doesn't want **money for nothing**, only help to stay working.
